strengths: Introduces InterRVOS, a new interaction-aware referring video object segmentation task that explicitly models actor-target roles rather than only isolated target objects.

Provides InterRVOS-8K, a large-scale dataset with 127K referring expressions across 8.7K videos. It is the first RVOS dataset to annotate actor-target interactions and includes diverse expression types (appearance, motion, multi-instance, class-level).

Dataset utility is supported by transfer experiments: training on InterRVOS-2K/5K outperforms the larger Ref-SAV dataset on the MeViS benchmark in both joint-training and zero-shot settings (Table 3), and generalizes to standard RVOS benchmarks (Table A2).

The proposed ReVIOSa baseline extends SAM2 + InternVL with [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens, and ablation in Table 6 shows that joint actor-target supervision improves performance over single-token or independently supervised variants.
The appendix provides extensive implementation details, annotation prompts, dataset statistics, and qualitative examples, which improves clarity and reproducibility relative to many dataset papers.
weaknesses: The dataset is automatically annotated with GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B but lacks human verification or quality control. No caption correctness, hallucination rate, role-label accuracy, or mask-caption alignment evaluation is reported, so the reliability of the interaction annotations and benchmark is uncertain.

The architectural contribution is incremental: ReVIOSa is essentially an existing multimodal LLM plus SAM2 with two special segmentation tokens and LoRA fine-tuning. The method does not deeply model interaction structure beyond token-level role conditioning, and the novelty relative to Sa2VA is limited.

The token design does not clearly handle multi-target or bidirectional interactions. [SEG_TAR] is singular, yet Figure 3 includes one actor with multiple targets (e.g., Actor [2] / Target [0], [1]). The paper does not explain how multiple target masks are generated or evaluated, and bidirectional interactions are handled with only [SEG_ACT], despite requiring segmentation of multiple interacting entities.

The evaluation protocol and dataset splits are not fully specified. Experiments use InterRVOS-2K, InterRVOS-5K, and InterRVOS-8K without clearly defining training/validation splits, and the actor-target metric details (how J&F is aggregated over multiple masks or multiple targets) are missing.

Baseline comparisons in Table 5 may be unfair: it is unclear whether ReferFormer, LMPM, and Sa2VA were trained on the same InterRVOS data and under comparable budgets. The overall gain over Sa2VA-4B is small (59.7 vs. 58.5), and no statistical significance or variance across runs is reported.

The paper claims state-of-the-art performance, but this is on the authors' newly introduced automatically annotated benchmark. Stronger evidence would include human-verified evaluation, comparison to human upper bounds, or broader external validation.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated task, interaction-aware referring video object segmentation (InterRVOS), that broadens RVOS beyond isolated single-target localization to explicitly model actor–target roles and inter-object relations, which is an underexplored and meaningful direction for video understanding.

Contributes InterRVOS-8K, the largest annotated RVOS dataset to date (127K referring expressions over 8,738 videos), constructed with a transparent four-stage automatic pipeline (GPT-4o + LLaMA-70B) and with paired actor/target expressions that provide a new supervision signal; the dataset statistics and Appendix C/D provide reasonable evidence of scale and diversity.

Proposes a concrete baseline (ReVIOSa) built on InternVL-2.5 + SAM2 with dedicated [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens, and demonstrates through ablations (Table 6) that joint actor–target supervision outperforms both a single [SEG] token and independent training, supporting the claim that role-aware modeling helps.

Empirical results are competitive: ReVIOSa-1B/4B attains state-of-the-art overall J&F on InterRVOS-8K (Table 5), and notably the 1B model surpasses the much larger Sa2VA-4B on interaction metrics, which is a non-trivial data-efficiency result.

The dataset-quality argument is supported by controlled experiments (Tables 3, 4, A1, A2): training on InterRVOS-5K yields better zero-shot generalization to MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS than training on larger Ref-SAV, providing evidence that interaction-centric supervision is beneficial beyond the proposed benchmark.

The paper is clearly written, the task definition is precise, the annotation prompts are fully disclosed in the Appendix (Figures A7–A13), and the evaluation protocol (Table 5) and evaluation-set construction are described, which aids reproducibility.
Introduces an actor-target-aware evaluation setting that specifically measures role-sensitive segmentation, complementing the standard referring setting and enabling more targeted comparison.
weaknesses: The dataset is built automatically with GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B, and while prompt details are given, there is limited quantitative validation of annotation quality (e.g., human verification rates, inter-annotator agreement, or error analysis on the interaction labels); the reliability of automatically generated role assignments and captions is central to the paper's claims and would benefit from more rigorous validation.

Source videos come exclusively from VidOR, so the diversity of interaction types is inherited from a single dataset and may be biased toward certain social/human-centric scenes; this limits claims about general interaction coverage.

The architecture is largely a composition of existing components (InternVL-2.5 + LoRA + SAM2 decoder) with two new prompt tokens; the methodological novelty is modest and the performance gains over Sa2VA-4B are small in some categories (e.g., Table 5 overall 60.0 vs 58.5), making the architectural contribution less compelling than the dataset contribution.

The claim that training with both actor and target supervision improves performance even in standard RVOS settings is asserted but only weakly isolated; a cleaner ablation that separates interaction data from joint-token supervision would strengthen this argument.

Failure-case analysis is thin: the paper reports safeguards in the annotation prompts but does not characterize how often the pipeline mislabels actor/target roles or fails for bidirectional/multi-object interactions, nor how such errors propagate into downstream training and metrics.
Evaluation is limited to a small set of benchmarks, and comparisons on standard RVOS are not always at matched parameter counts or training budgets, making some equivalences harder to interpret.
Some qualitative panels (Figures 5, A4–A6) show only successful cases, which risks underrepresenting systematic failure modes of the proposed pipeline.

strengths: Introduces InterRVOS, a new interaction-aware referring video object segmentation task that requires segmenting both actor and target entities from complementary referring expressions, extending standard actor-only RVOS.

Constructs InterRVOS-8K, a large-scale automatically annotated dataset (127K expressions, 8.7K videos, 17.7K actor-target interactions) with diverse expression types including single-object, multi-instance, motion-only, and interaction-aware cases.

Proposes a baseline architecture, ReVIOSa, that uses special [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] tokens to jointly segment actor and target roles, and reports state-of-the-art results on the proposed benchmark together with data-efficiency gains on MeViS.

Provides an actor-target-aware evaluation setting and extensive supplementary material, including annotation prompts, dataset statistics, qualitative examples, and zero-shot comparisons, which improves transparency of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The dataset is constructed automatically with GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B, but no human verification or quality-control study is reported for the generated referring expressions, interaction labels, or mask alignment. This is a material concern because the main contribution is the dataset, and annotation errors or hallucinated interactions would directly affect all downstream claims.

The source annotations in VidOR are primarily bounding boxes/relations, not pixel-level segmentation masks, yet the paper does not clearly explain how segmentation masks are obtained. This makes the dataset construction insufficiently reproducible and raises questions about the reliability of the ground-truth masks used for training and evaluation.

The proposed architecture is largely a combination of existing components (SAM2, InternVL/LLaVA, LoRA, special segmentation tokens), similar in spirit to prior LISA/GLaMM-style works. The technical novelty of the baseline is limited, and the reported gains over Sa2VA are modest in several settings.

Experimental comparisons on the proposed InterRVOS-8K benchmark are limited to a few baselines, and the paper does not include strong standard RVOS methods (e.g., ReferFormer, MTTR, or recent specialized RVOS models) in the main quantitative comparison, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art interaction modeling.

The generated referring expressions frequently use generic terms such as "object" and may not reflect natural human language, but the paper does not evaluate whether models perform differently on naturalistic expressions or whether the automatic captions introduce systematic biases.

The model's behavior in standard RVOS settings is not deeply analyzed: it must dynamically decide whether to emit [SEG_TAR], yet there is little analysis of when this fails or how often unnecessary target segmentation is produced, especially on benchmarks without interaction annotations.

There are presentation/reproducibility issues, including inconsistency about the multimodal language model backbone (LLaVA vs. InternVL-2.5), the missing project URL, and insufficient details on dataset release, mask generation, and annotation validation.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated task, Interaction-aware RVOS, that explicitly models the asymmetric actor/target roles in interactions rather than only segmenting a single referred object; this addresses an underexplored aspect of RVOS.

Contributes InterRVOS-127K, a large-scale dataset (127K expressions, ~17.6K interaction annotations) with distinct actor and target masks, which is the first of its kind for interaction-aware referring segmentation and meaningfully extends existing RVOS benchmarks.

The ReVIOSa architecture (interaction-aware [SEG_ACT]/[SEG_TAR] tokens plus attention mask loss) is sensible, and its components are supported by a clean ablation (Table 4: baseline 57.0 -> 62.0 J&F) as well as a layer/head selection analysis.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: it reports results on the proposed InterRVOS-Actor/Target benchmarks, standard RVOS benchmarks, zero-shot generalization (Table A3), dataset-efficiency comparisons (Table A2), and qualitative actor-target joint segmentation (Figs. 5, A10, A11).

The paper is generally well-organized and clearly written, with informative figures (task definition, pipeline, architecture) and detailed appendix documentation of the annotation pipeline and prompts.
weaknesses: The dataset is built fully automatically with GPT-4o/LLaMA-70B and masks pre-computed by SAM2, and only the evaluation set was human-refined. The quality of the 'ground-truth' masks and expressions is not quantitatively validated (no human agreement / annotation-quality study), which is a critical concern for a segmentation benchmark. Since the model also relies on SAM2 for masks, there is a potential circularity between the automatically generated targets and the evaluated predictions.

The central new capability (target segmentation) cannot be fairly compared against prior methods, since all baselines are reported as '-' on InterRVOS-Target. Consequently, the strongest evidence for the new task rests on the authors' own model, weakening the empirical case that the task is well-defined and solvable.

Architectural novelty is modest: the MLLM + SAM2 + special-token + LoRA framework is largely inherited from prior works (e.g., LISA, Sa2VA). The main new elements are the two role tokens and the attention mask loss, which are incremental extensions of existing [SEG]-token designs.

The attention mask loss layer/head selection (top-1 layer, top-4 heads) is purely heuristic and empirically tuned; the paper does not show that the chosen configuration transfers across backbones/scales (only 1B and 4B of the same family are examined), limiting claims of generality.

There is no direct comparison against concurrent multi-object/interaction grounding approaches (e.g., GCC, ReasonVOS) despite these being discussed as related, and no human evaluation of expression naturalness/diversity to substantiate the claimed richness of the annotations.

Some comparisons mix model scales (1B/4B vs. 7B/13B baselines), and the reported gains on standard RVOS are modest; the practical significance of the interaction-aware formulation over standard RVOS in terms of downstream utility is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Introduces InterRVOS, a well-motivated new task that extends standard RVOS by requiring separate segmentation of actor and target objects from a single interaction expression, with an accompanying evaluation protocol. This addresses an underexplored aspect of RVOS: modeling asymmetric object roles in interactions.

Presents InterRVOS-127K, a large-scale dataset with over 127K expressions, 8,738 videos, and actor-target annotations. The automatic annotation pipeline built on VidOR, SAM2, GPT-4o, and LLaMA is described in detail, and the dataset includes both interaction-aware and standard referring expressions, making it a useful resource.

Proposes ReVIOSa, a sensible MLLM-based architecture with interaction-aware special tokens [SEG_ACT] and [SEG_TAR] and an attention mask loss (AML) to align attention maps with actor/target masks. Ablation studies show both components improve performance, and the layer/head selection analysis provides useful insight into MLLM attention behavior.

Empirical results are strong: ReVIOSa achieves state-of-the-art performance on InterRVOS-127K and remains competitive on standard RVOS benchmarks (MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS, Ref-DAVIS). Zero-shot and data-efficiency experiments in the appendix further support the value of the interaction-centric dataset.

Reproducibility is generally good: implementation details, training settings, annotation prompts, layer/head selection strategy, and dataset statistics are provided in the main paper and appendix, with a project page referenced.
weaknesses: The quality of the automatically annotated training data is not rigorously validated. Expressions and masks are generated by GPT-4o, LLaMA, and SAM2, but the paper reports no human verification of the training split, no inter-annotator agreement, and no annotation error-rate analysis. Since the dataset is a central contribution, this is a meaningful concern.

The treatment of bidirectional interactions is ambiguous. Stage 3 states that bidirectional interactions are extracted 'without role assignment,' yet the task and dataset claim actor-target annotations and separate evaluation for actor and target. It is unclear how bidirectional samples are handled in the InterRVOS-Actor/Target evaluation and whether all interaction expressions truly have distinct actor/target roles.

Baseline comparison for InterRVOS-Target is limited. Existing RVOS methods cannot produce target masks, so the target evaluation only reports ReVIOSa. A simple multi-token baseline or an adapted prior method would better contextualize the difficulty of the new task. The actor comparison also mainly uses standard RVOS baselines that are not designed for interaction expressions.

The paper does not quantify the accuracy of the model's inference-time decision of whether an expression involves an interaction and whether to emit [SEG_TAR]. Errors in this token-selection step could significantly affect role-specific segmentation, but they are not analyzed.

Ablations are performed only with the 1B model; the 4B model lacks component analysis. Additionally, standard RVOS evaluation uses a variant without interaction-aware tokens, so the full model's generalization to standard RVOS is not directly measured.

strengths: Introduces a new task, InterRVOS, that extends referring video object segmentation by requiring separate segmentation of actor and target objects in interaction expressions. This is a meaningful formulation that goes beyond single-object RVOS and could support human-object interaction understanding.

Constructs InterRVOS-127K, a large-scale dataset with over 127K expressions, 35K objects, and distinct actor-target mask annotations. The dataset supports both interaction-aware and standard RVOS settings, and the automatic annotation pipeline is described in detail.

Proposes ReVIOSa with interaction-aware special tokens ([SEG_ACT], [SEG_TAR]) and an attention mask loss. Ablations in Table 4 show that both components improve performance over the baseline, and qualitative examples demonstrate joint actor-target segmentation.

Provides useful analyses, including attention layer-head selection, attention mask visualization, and dataset statistics. Zero-shot evaluations on standard RVOS benchmarks (Tables A1-A3) suggest that training on InterRVOS-127K can transfer to conventional RVOS datasets.
weaknesses: The dataset quality is not adequately validated. The training set is automatically annotated using GPT-4o and LLaMA without human verification, error analysis, or inter-annotator agreement. Interaction labels, actor/target role assignments, and expression correctness may be noisy or hallucinated, which is a critical issue for a new benchmark. Only the evaluation set is human-refined, but noisy training labels can affect both the proposed model and any baselines trained on the dataset.

Baseline comparisons in Table 2 are not apples-to-apples. Prior methods such as ReferFormer, LMPM, VISA, VideoLISA, and Sa2VA are not trained on InterRVOS-127K, while ReVIOSa is trained on it. The paper does not specify that baselines were fine-tuned on the new dataset, so the reported gains may simply reflect in-domain training. For InterRVOS-Target, no baselines are reported at all, making the target-segmentation results unverified.

The evaluation may not actually measure interaction understanding. Interaction expressions often syntactically encode the actor and target (e.g., 'A throwing B'), so a model can parse the sentence and segment two nouns without modeling visual interaction dynamics. There is no counterfactual or role-swap evaluation, and no explicit metric for whether the model assigns actor/target roles correctly. A model that swaps the two masks could still obtain high separate J&F scores if both masks are otherwise accurate.

The method contribution is incremental. ReVIOSa adds two special tokens and an attention mask loss to an existing MLLM + SAM2 pipeline. Attention supervision is a known technique, and the architecture is close to prior LISA/Grounded-SAM-style approaches. The main novelty is the dataset and task, while the technical method itself is relatively straightforward.

There are clarity and reproducibility concerns. The main text says the MLLM is LLaVA-based, but the appendix states InternVL-2.5 is used; the main text cites LLaMA-70B, while the appendix refers to a quantized LLaMA 3.1 Instruct model. It is also unclear how the special tokens are supervised by the text loss. The annotation pipeline depends on proprietary GPT-4o, which limits reproducibility.

The standard RVOS evaluation uses only a variant with attention mask loss, not the full ReVIOSa with interaction-aware special tokens, because the tokens are not compatible with standard RVOS. Thus the claimed strong performance on standard RVOS benchmarks does not validate the full architecture. In Table A1, ReVIOSa-4B is also worse than Sa2VA-4B on Ref-DAVIS (71.6 vs 73.8).

The paper lacks a detailed analysis of ambiguity in actor/target role assignment. Many interaction expressions may have multiple plausible targets or reciprocal interactions, and it is unclear how the dataset defines the 'correct' target mask in such cases. The dataset statistics (e.g., 65% of videos contain interaction expressions) do not resolve how many expressions are interaction-based or how target masks are validated.
